enrichment.short_title: Costs where nominal winner lost on principle
key_facts: Mr Islam ran Mrs Ali's late husband's accountancy practice for 26 months and claimed about £156,000 on hourly-rate and profit-retention bases.
The judge found Mrs Ali's reasonable-remuneration case succeeded in principle and awarded only £12,746 after credits for sums already received.
Mrs Ali had made a lower Part 36-style settlement proposal than Mr Islam's, but the judge ordered Mr Islam his costs as the monetary winner.
The Court of Appeal held Mrs Ali had effectively won the substantive dispute and substituted no order as to costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court costs order following judgment for the claimant on quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; no order as to costs substituted for the judge's costs order; appellant's appeal costs summarily assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Where the final monetary award is very small compared with the sums in dispute and the defendant succeeded on the determinative issues of principle, a trial judge may err in treating the claimant as the successful party for costs; the court may substitute no order as to costs.
legal_issues: Who was the successful party for CPR Part 44.3 costs purposes
Whether comparison of Part 36 offers justified depriving the claimant of costs
When the Court of Appeal may interfere with a judge's costs discretion
Effect of winning on principle but recovering only a small balance

enrichment.short_title: Restored company and limitation after dissolution
key_facts: Regent Leisuretime was struck off and dissolved in 1998 after defaulting on a NatWest loan secured on property valuations said to meet a £3.5m forced-sale requirement.
Directors restored the company without notice in 2001 and immediately sued the bank for fraudulent misrepresentation over the 1992 valuation.
District Judge Walker gave a limitation direction suspending time during dissolution; HHJ Overend deleted it and granted summary judgment on limitation.
The Court of Appeal held the bank could intervene, the limitation direction was rightly deleted, and the company's claim was statute-barred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against orders varying a restoration order and granting summary judgment on limitation in the company's misrepresentation claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; company liable for costs from Judge Overend onwards.
enrichment.ratio: A bank prejudiced by a limitation direction on restoration may be heard; jurisdiction exists to suspend limitation for a restored company only in exceptional cases; directors' knowledge of fraud before dissolution is the company's knowledge, so section 32 Limitation Act 1980 does not revive a claim barred by September 1999.
legal_issues: Whether third parties may apply to vary a restoration order
Jurisdiction under section 653(3) to suspend limitation for the restored company
Whether a misrepresentation claim is based upon fraud for section 32(1)(a)
When a lender's cause of action in negligent valuation accrues

enrichment.short_title: Barnstaple bypass and bird habitat directives
key_facts: Mr Bown challenged confirmation of compulsory purchase and highway orders for the Barnstaple Western Bypass bridge over the Taw-Torridge estuary SSSI.
He argued the estuary should have been designated an SPA under the Wild Birds Directive and that otter disturbance would breach the Habitats Regulations.
English Nature and JNCC guidance showed the site no longer met published SPA selection criteria despite earlier IBA listings.
Collins J dismissed both grounds and summarily assessed part of the defendant's costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's confirmation of highway and compulsory purchase orders after a public inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; summary assessment of £2,268.75 for non-legally-aided costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to designate a site as an SPA does not make development unlawful where authoritative scientific material shows it does not meet selection criteria; an inspector may rely on planning conditions and mitigation rather than pre-deciding Regulation 44 licensing criteria for otters.
legal_issues: Whether non-designation of an IBA-listed estuary as an SPA rendered the bridge unlawful
Application of Article 4 Wild Birds Directive where Member State has not classified an SPA
Whether otter disturbance required Regulation 44 assessment before order confirmation
Weight of JNCC SPA selection guidelines against historic IBA inventories

enrichment.short_title: Pig movement records and burden of proof
key_facts: Alan Hall Clement was convicted of 14 offences relating to pig movements from West Craig Lea to Thompson's abattoir and failure to produce movement records.
The magistrates treated Schedule 5 pre-movement declarations as satisfying Schedule 1 holding records and relied on defence submissions as factual admissions.
Silber J held Schedule 5 forms did not satisfy Schedule 1 because they record intended rather than completed movements.
The magistrates also misdirected themselves that the prosecution need only prove a prima facie case before the burden reverted to the defence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' convictions under the Pigs Order and Animal Health Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; all 14 convictions quashed; defendant's costs order out of central funds.
enrichment.ratio: A Schedule 5 declaration of intended movement within seven days is not substantially to the like effect of a Schedule 1 record of completed movement; counsel's legal submissions are not admissions of fact; save for lawful authority or excuse under Article 16, the prosecution must prove every element beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_issues: Whether Schedule 5 records satisfy Schedule 1 record-keeping requirements
Whether defence submissions on form equivalence could prove ownership or charge
Sufficiency of evidence identifying the defendant's signature on Schedule 5 forms
Correct allocation of burden of proof under Article 16

confidence.notes: Short, clear case stated decision on statutory form requirements and burden of proof.

enrichment.short_title: Singapore relocation of children after divorce
key_facts: A Singaporean mother sought leave to relocate two boys aged 11 and 8 to Singapore; the English father opposed and cross-applied for residence.
The parents separated in 1999; the mother felt isolated in England and the children were distressed by contact disputes and the father's new relationship.
Expert evidence emphasised the mother's unhappiness as central but did not recommend a firm outcome; neither expert favoured one option conclusively.
Charles J granted relocation on the basis refusal was unlikely to improve the mother's mood and would harm the children's welfare.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court hearing of the mother's application for leave to remove children from the jurisdiction and the father's cross-application for a residence order.
enrichment.outcome: Mother granted permission to relocate to Singapore with mirror-order undertaking as to contact; father did not pursue residence if mother remained in England.
enrichment.ratio: Following Payne v Payne, there is no presumption in favour of relocation, but where a genuine primary carer's proposal is realistic and refusal is unlikely to secure her happiness and stability, permission may best promote the child's welfare even though contact with the left-behind parent will reduce.
legal_issues: Application of Payne v Payne guidance to an isolated expatriate primary carer
Whether the mother's application was genuine or motivated by spite
Likely effect on children of relocation versus compelled stay in England
Weight to be given to reduced paternal contact against maternal stability

confidence.notes: Full reserved judgment applying Payne with detailed welfare analysis and clear grant of leave.

key_facts: David Weller strangled his girlfriend Ziggy Fisher after she tried to end their possessive relationship; the sole issue was murder or provocation manslaughter.
Following R v Smith (Morgan), defence counsel sought a direction that the jury could take Weller's jealousy and possessiveness into account on the objective limb.
The judge directed the jury to consider all circumstances and what society expects of a man in the defendant's position, but omitted that phrase on repetition after a jury note.
The Court of Appeal held the combined directions left jealousy open for consideration and the conviction was safe.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave of the full court against conviction for murder following trial at Bristol Crown Court.
enrichment.ratio: After Smith (Morgan), the judge must not tell the jury to ignore defendant characteristics on the section 3 objective question, but need not expressly list jealousy; directing the jury to apply community standards to a man in the defendant's position can suffice, and an omitted phrase on repetition does not necessarily render the conviction unsafe.
legal_issues: Proper jury direction on provocation after R v Smith (Morgan)
Whether jealousy and possessiveness must be expressly left to the jury
Effect of incomplete repetition of a provocation summing-up
Distinction between subjective loss of control and excusability of loss of control

confidence.notes: Focused appellate judgment on post-Smith provocation directions with clear dismissal.

key_facts: Michael Frost, aged 17, killed a 75-year-old family friend who had sexually abused him; at trial he ran provocation and self-defence only.
A 1998 appeal on provocation directions failed; the CCRC referred the case after fresh psychiatric evidence from Dr Misch and Dr Bester.
Both psychiatrists agreed depression, adjustment disorder and PTSD substantially impaired his mental responsibility at the time of the killing.
The Crown accepted fresh evidence should be admitted and that a manslaughter plea would likely have been accepted at trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder conviction following CCRC reference and admission of fresh psychiatric evidence under section 23 Criminal Appeal Act 1968.
enrichment.outcome: Murder conviction quashed; substituted conviction for manslaughter on grounds of diminished responsibility; sentence seven years' imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh psychiatric evidence showing abnormality of mind substantially impairing responsibility may be admitted where diminished responsibility was not tactically run at trial and there is a reasonable explanation for non-disclosure of the full abuse history; where agreed expert evidence establishes diminished responsibility, a murder conviction is unsafe.
legal_issues: Admission of fresh psychiatric evidence on CCRC reference
Whether failure to run diminished responsibility at trial was tactical
Reasonableness of late disclosure of extent of sexual abuse
Appropriate substitute sentence after quashing murder conviction

confidence.notes: Clear CCRC appeal with agreed expert evidence and substituted verdict; anonymised defendant initials in case name.

enrichment.short_title: Discretionary lifer review date set by Secretary of State
key_facts: Mr Clough was detained at Her Majesty's Pleasure for aggravated arson with a three-year relevant period; he absconded twice from open conditions.
In July 2002 the Discretionary Lifer Panel recommended transfer to open conditions and review nine months after transfer.
The Secretary of State accepted transfer but fixed the next review at 15 months, citing need to demonstrate fitness for release.
Grigson J upheld the Secretary of State's power to set review timing and held 15 months was not unreasonable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision to defer the next Parole Board review beyond the Panel's recommended interval.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal granted subject to stay pending R (Spence) in the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Section 28(7) Crime (Sentences) Act 1997 gives the Secretary of State exclusive control over referral timing subject to the two-year fail-safe trigger; varying a Panel recommendation on when to test open conditions is an executive judgment on prison management and risk reduction, reviewable only for unreasonableness and compatible with Article 5(4) reasonable intervals.
legal_issues: Whether the prisoner has a right to require referral at the Panel's recommended date
Compatibility with Article 5(4) and Article 6 access to court
Whether fixing a 15-month rather than 9-month interval was Wednesbury unreasonable
Distinction between release decisions and administrative timing of review

linked_authorities.name: R (Spence) v Secretary of State for the Home Department
R v Lord Chancellor ex parte Witham

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment on section 28 timing powers; source metadata lists multiple judges beyond Grigson J.

enrichment.short_title: CCRC murder appeal and time of death
key_facts: Harold Williams was convicted in 1977 of murdering Margaret Davies, his former partner, in a circumstantial case turning on time of death.
He had a partial alibi until about 11.50 pm on Friday and from 7.45 am Saturday; pathologists placed death before 6 am Saturday.
The CCRC referred the case because a lay witness said she saw the deceased on Saturday morning and Professor Crane questioned knife evidence.
The Court of Appeal admitted Mrs Hall's evidence and Professor Crane's report but dismissed the appeal under Pendleton principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder conviction following CCRC reference, continued after the appellant's death by his sister under section 44A.
enrichment.ratio: On a CCRC reference, new evidence must be assessed by whether it might reasonably have affected the jury's verdict; consensus of pathologists that death likely occurred before 6 am Saturday undermines a lay witness's Saturday sighting, and challenges to trial knife evidence add little to a strong circumstantial case.
legal_issues: Admissibility of fresh lay and expert evidence on time of death
Whether Mrs Hall's Saturday sighting was credible
Impact of Professor Crane's views on the murder weapon
Application of R v Pendleton safety test to CCRC references

confidence.notes: Full CCRC appeal judgment with explicit Pendleton analysis and dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: EIA screening and contaminated land remediation

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Assessment of Environmental Effects) Regulations 1988

key_facts: The Secretary of State granted full planning permission for 407 residential units on the contaminated Harford Street Gasworks site in Stepney.
Mr Gillespie successfully challenged the permission at first instance because no environmental impact assessment was carried out.
The developer submitted outline remediation reports and Condition VI required detailed investigation and an approved remediation scheme before works began.
The Court of Appeal held the Secretary of State could consider remedial measures when screening, but erred by treating Condition VI as assuming successful remediation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by the developer against quashing of planning permission for failure to conduct EIA screening properly.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; planning permission remains quashed; developer ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: When screening urban development under the 1988 Regulations, proposed integral remedial measures may be considered, but where contamination extent and remediation are uncertain and deferred to conditions, the decision-maker cannot assume future investigations will succeed and thereby conclude significant environmental effects are unlikely; unresolved remediation contingencies require EIA.
legal_issues: Whether proposed remediation measures may be taken into account at EIA screening
Distinction between standard mitigation and elaborate contaminated-land remediation
Whether Condition VI could substitute for an environmental statement
Correct test for likely significant environmental effects on brownfield gasworks land
